newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Attack fears prompt Cambodian PM to cancel mission.
newsitem.headline: Attack fears prompt Cambodian PM to cancel mission.

text.p: Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh cancelled a trip to Ta Sanh, a base for Khmer Rouge defectors, on Monday over fears rebels loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen would attack him, senior army officers said.
The uneasy coalition between Ranariddh and Hun Sen has deteriorated as the two leaders compete for the loyalty of the Khmer Rouge rebels and control of the divided armed forces.

"There is no safety or security here. According to the police and soldiers here there is a threat from the local commander (of Khmer Rouge defectors)," said Lieutenant-General Nhiek Bun Chhay, deputy chief of staff for the armed forces.
Several soldiers in this northwest district of Samlaut called the situation "very, very tense", and villagers said they had been blocked from trying to welcome Ranariddh.
Nhiek Bun Chhay said fears over the prince's safety prompted him to telephone Ranariddh, who was about to board a helicopter at Phnom Penh's Pochentong Airport, and recommend he cancel his flight.
Police in the in the northwest town of Battambang said they had intercepted radio transmissions that suggested Ranariddh's life was in danger.
"We heard people say, 'Are the helicopters to be shot down?' and then someone answered, 'No, wait for the order. But please have your artillery ready'," a police official told reporters.
The cancellation of Ranariddh's trip comes 10 days after Hun Sen led a triumphant tour in Samlaut.

During Hun Sen's visit, thousands of former Khmer Rouge rebels pledged their loyalty to his ex-communist Cambodian People's Party (CPP) in what analysts said was the strongest sign yet that recruitment of Khmer Rouge, who led the brutal 1975-1979 "killing fields regime", has become a highly partisan.
Military analysts said they believed 99 percent of Samlaut is controlled by the CPP.

"I am very sorry that it seems that territory and loyalty is divided between Funcinpec and CPP. Why can't the prince, who is the head of the government and army, visit here?" Nhiek Bun Chhay told reporters. Funcipec is Ranariddh's party.

Uoch Vorn, a 30-year-old woman, said she had walked 30 km (19 miles) to greet Ranariddh in Ta Sanh. "I had to pass 10 checkpoints stopping me. Soldiers said the situation was bad and there would be fighting," she said.
Ei Chien, a leading Khmer Rouge defector from the northwest town of Pailin, said he had come with several dozen troops to provide security for Ranariddh's visit.
"I think there are tensions because the other side doesn't want people to come greet the prince. They threatened people...and I would like to appeal for troops to cooperate with each other," he said.

Chea Mon, deputy secretary of a division of defectors based in Ta Sanh, said that the Pailin troops were not welcome. "We don't understand why they are here," he said. "There are more than 100 with weapons."
The Khmer Rouge have been hit by massive defections in recent months, leaving only between 800 and 2,000 hardliners in the northwest jungle base of Anlong Veng.
After being forced from power by a Vietnamese invasion in 1979, the Khmer Rouge fought a Hanoi-installed regime before signing a U.N.-brokered peace pact in 1991.
They later reneged on the treaty and have been fighting the coalition government since its installation after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.
